extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of literature and philosophy; readers of Montaigne
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria implicit in Montaigne's personal essays for composing or judging candid, reflective, philosophical prose about the self and society. Emphasizes candour, memory, education, judgment, and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak what you think (candour over dissembling)
rubrics_metrics.description: “What a man says should be what he thinks... otherwise ‘tis knavery.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not eternally counterfeit and dissemble; prefer being troublesome and indiscreet to being a flatterer or dissembler. Montaigne asserts candour as a moral and practical virtue: dissimulation makes one not believed even when telling the truth and destroys genuine conversation. Example: princes who brag of hiding intentions invite distrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep faith; avoid the first breach of word
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking faith for immediate gain creates long-term disrepute and distrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although gain may tempt a prince to once break his word, that first breach has infinite mischievous consequences, excluding him from future negotiation. Example: Soliman ordered the release of prisoners surrendered contrary to capitulation to preserve future confidence. Policy: consider long-term reputational costs over short-term advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer candour as a habitual practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne declares: he abandons himself to candour, always to speak as he thinks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack artifice, memory, or assurance to feign, adopt openness deliberately. Cited advantage: Aristippus said philosophy’s principal benefit was speaking freely and openly to all. Practical note: candour may appear indiscreet but preserves integrity and consistency of judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory is essential to judgment and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “Memory is a faculty of wonderful use, and without which the judgment can very hardly perform its office.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize memory limits and compensate (notes, committing speeches to writing). Montaigne describes practical strategies (notebook, learning by heart) and the costs when memory fails (forgetting sources, one’s own writings). Teaching/learning implication: do not over-rely on unaided recollection; use external aids and accept their effects on composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately attribute and acknowledge sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne frequently forgets authorship and is ‘very often quoted to myself’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because memory is treacherous, be cautious in attribution and value concurrence of authority with reason. When possible, record sources; accept that failing to attribute undermines learning’s social validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value universality and readiness of the soul over narrow skill
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beautiful souls are they that are universal, open, and ready for all things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admire and cultivate broad capacities rather than a single narrow excellence. While every soul may show a particular faculty, true beauty lies in general openness and capability across matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should make us good and wise, not merely learned
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne criticizes that education 'has not taught us to follow and embrace virtue and prudence, but she has imprinted in us their derivation and etymology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer curricula and instruction that change judgment and manners and promote practical virtue (Polemon’s reformation after hearing Xenocrates) rather than teaching fine language and verbal erudition alone. Select texts for moral and practical effect, not only rhetorical elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence: preserve established, constant institutions over disruptive change
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne finds instability the worst thing in the state and prefers 'any old government better than change and alteration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing institutions, weigh the difficulty and danger of reformation; do not lightly stir established customs—better to keep a long-standing, imperfect order than to unsettle society without a reliable replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain authenticity; do not imitate others at cost to yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Value ‘aequabilitas’—order and equability of life; 'which thou canst not possibly observe if, imitating other men’s natures, thou layest aside thy own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek steadiness and correspondence in opinions and manners rather than striking, imitative actions. Authentic consistency is superior to borrowed brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise independent, fair judgement about others
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne will 'give my very enemies their due testimony of honour' and keeps affection separate from judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let passion obscure assessment; be ready to praise what merits praise, condemn faults honestly, and avoid attributing unearned qualities. Maintain liberty of judgement even toward friends and enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize human reason’s ambivalence and the value of humility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Human reason is a two-edged and dangerous sword... it has many several points.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that reason can support opposing conclusions; be cautious in asserting certainty. Where appearances balance, one may legitimately defer, even to chance, rather than force a dubious determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisiveness is a virtue; irresolution is a blemish
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne confesses 'irresolution; a very great effect and very incommodious in the negotiations of the affairs of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although human judgment often balances, indecision impedes action. When balanced reasons make choice difficult, recognize the cost of irresolution and consider decisive methods (commitment, delegation, or even lot) to resolve matters practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical knowledge matters; erudition without practical skills is incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne lists his ignorance of husbandry, mechanic arts, merchandise, and everyday practicalities despite learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure education and personal competence not only by learned names and fine expressions but by practical ability in life’s necessary tasks; avoid the vanity of being learned without being useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in commendation and disdain for vain self-regard
rubrics_metrics.description: People readily claim sufficiency of sense; 'there never was porter or the silliest girl, that did not think they had sense enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate humility about one’s own judgement; recognize the common tendency to overestimate one’s understanding. When evaluating work or persons, be aware of this bias and temper praise accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness in literary craft (implicit rule for poetry/writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bookmark aphorism: 'A man may play the fool in everything else, but not in poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In artistic composition, avoid frivolity; poetry (and by extension serious literary expression) demands a gravity and care that excuses less trivial behaviour than ordinary conduct. Ensure craft and earnestness in literary effort.
